channel.title: Chrome Web Platform Ecosystem Updates
channel.description: Weekly web intelligence on ChromeStatus features, web standards, and developer community pulse

item.title: HTML-in-canvas — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
HTML-in-canvas (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

HTML-in-canvas enables customizing the rendering of html using canvas with new primitives to manage canvas layout, drawing capabilities, rendering events for DOM-to-canvas synchronization, and geometry update capabilities for canvas-to-DOM synchronization.

Ecosystem Analysis: HTML-in-canvas has shipped enabled by default in Chrome 157, providing long-awaited primitives like `drawElementImage` and geometry updates to render live, accessible DOM subtrees directly inside 2D, WebGL, and WebGPU canvas pipelines. The developer ecosystem has moved rapidly with early integration into graphics engines like Babylon.js and PixiJS. Cross-browser consensus is developing, with WebKit signaling support for the immediate-mode API design while Gecko continues evaluating privacy edge-cases alongside active WPT test synchronization.

item.title: Decisions API — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Decisions API (Chrome 157, In developer trial (Behind a flag))

Provides high-speed, deterministic semantic decision-making directly on the user's device as a built-in AI capability. Unlike open-ended generative language models (such as the Prompt API) that decode text token-by-token over hundreds or thousands of milliseconds, the Decisions API (window.DecisionModel) evaluates natural language input text against a structured set of questions and candidate options in a single forward pass using logit scoring. This delivers micro-latency evaluations (tens or low hundreds of milliseconds on typical consumer laptop CPUs and GPUs) while outputting calibrated confidence values. This brings non-autoregressive "System 1" decision models (e.g. Jev, Laya, Kev, Open-Jev) natively into the web platform, providing developers with a pragmatic, zero-marginal-cost "Semantic If" primitive for real-time client-side routing, interactive input guardrails, and adaptive user interfaces.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Decisions API (window.DecisionModel) is an experimental on-device Built-in AI capability introduced in Chromium (Chrome 157) behind a flag, introducing a deterministic 'Semantic If' primitive that scores text against structured schemas in a single forward pass without autoregressive token generation. Web developers see substantial utility in replacing heavy client-side LLMs and fragile heuristics for local triage and search facet routing, though the API is still an early proposal without formal web standards consensus. Broad interoperability remains distant as non-Chromium engines resist bundling platform-level inference weights into browser binaries.

item.title: Secure Payment Confirmation: Locale Validation — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Secure Payment Confirmation: Locale Validation (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Updates Secure Payment Confirmation's `locale` data field to return a Not Supported DOMException if none of the language tags provided in the field match the language used by the Secure Payment Confirmation's dialog. If the field is not set or empty, this validation is skipped. This helps web developers with matching the language of the data that they are supplying to Secure Payment Confirmation with the dialog.

Ecosystem Analysis: Secure Payment Confirmation (SPC) Locale Validation refines the W3C Web Payments specification by raising a NotSupportedError DOMException when none of the relying party's specified language tags match the browser dialog's active locale. Shipped enabled by default in Chrome 154, it prevents jarring language mismatches between merchant-supplied data and system confirmation prompts without exposing fingerprintable OS locale details. Despite its utility, broader ecosystem impact is constrained because full SPC implementation remains an almost exclusively Chromium-driven feature with no production support in Safari or Firefox.

item.title: Language Detector API on Android — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Language Detector API on Android (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Exposes the LanguageDetector JavaScript Web API on Chrome for Android (Clank). This allows web applications to detect text languages locally on mobile devices using fast, privacy-preserving, and offline-capable on-device machine learning models and not rely on cloud endpoints.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Language Detector API on Android extends Chromium's built-in, on-device AI capabilities to mobile devices, enabling fast, privacy-preserving, and offline-capable language identification without server roundtrips. While Chrome 157 enables the feature by default on Android to achieve parity with desktop, ecosystem interoperability remains single-engine due to objections from rival browser vendors.

item.title: CSS flow-start and flow-end alignment keywords — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS flow-start and flow-end alignment keywords (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

Introduce the flow-start/end keywords as value aliases for the existing flex-start/end keywords as resolved in the CSSWG. These are needed for alignment in the case of placement reversals. flow-start in CSS Grid-Lanes would indicate the starting edge of the container at which placement begins, which is useful in the case where placement is reversed (`fill-reverse`, `track-reverse`, discussed in this CSSWG issue: [css-grid-3][masonry] item-flow row vs. column in masonry layouts · Issue #12803 · w3c/csswg-drafts). Because these are acting as value aliases, we expect flex-start/end to follow the logical directions in Grid Lanes, as well, which will expand the definition of these keywords from only applying special behavior in flexbox to applying to any layout mode whose logical start/end is different from its physical start/end. For serialization, if either flex-start/end or flow-start/end is used, the returned serialized value should be flow-start/end.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS Working Group resolved to introduce flow-start and flow-end as canonical alignment keywords that alias legacy flex-start and flex-end across CSS Box Alignment Module Level 3 and CSS Grid Lanes. The feature solves alignment ambiguities when content placement is reversed (such as fill-reverse in masonry/grid-lanes layouts) while preserving container writing-mode semantics for start and end. With Chromium targeting enabled-by-default support in Chrome 158, Mozilla adopting an official positive stance, and WebKit reviewing the proposal without objection, engine consensus is solidly aligned.

item.title: FontFace width attribute and font-width descriptor — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
FontFace width attribute and font-width descriptor (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Exposes the width attribute on FontFace and the @font-face font-width descriptor as aliases for stretch and font-stretch. Aligns Chromium with the updated CSS Font Loading and CSS Fonts 4 specifications. Developers can now inspect or initialize font face widths using FontFace.width and CSS font-width interchangeably with stretch and font-stretch.

Ecosystem Analysis: The addition of the FontFace width attribute and the @font-face font-width descriptor aligns Chromium with the CSS Fonts 4 and CSS Font Loading specifications, formalizing width as the primary descriptor name while preserving stretch as a legacy alias. Following implementations in Safari and Firefox, Chrome's rollout achieves Baseline Newly Available status across all major browser engines and eliminates longstanding Web Platform Tests failures. The update represents an ergonomic, zero-friction spec modernization that fully maintains backwards compatibility with existing stylesheets.

item.title: Add javascriptURLs option to SanitizerConfig and Sanitizer — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Add javascriptURLs option to SanitizerConfig and Sanitizer (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/12898 Sanitizer API also sanitizes javascript:-URLs, when they are used for navigation. This was originally done as a side effect of any "safe" method that uses Sanitizer, and omittted for any "unsafe" method. The HTML standard recently regularized this and made this a developer-selectable option, instead of a side-effect of a particular method. Behaviour when the option is not used remains the same.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `javascriptURLs` option in `SanitizerConfig` and the accompanying `setJavascriptURLs()` method decouple `javascript:` URL sanitization from specific DOM insertion methods, making URL stripping an explicit, configurable setting rather than an implicit side-effect of 'safe' APIs. Formally merged into the WHATWG HTML standard and shipping enabled by default in Chrome 157, this change resolves a notable ergonomics problem for applications needing permissive parsing without forfeiting protection against script-based navigation. Engine consensus across Chromium, WebKit, and Gecko is firmly established, marking another solid step toward a mature, native Sanitizer API.

item.title: CSS text-decoration-inset — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS text-decoration-inset (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

CSS text-decoration-inset controls how far underlines, overlines, and line-through decorations are inset from or extended beyond text run edges. It supports auto, length, and percentage values, including one-value and two-value syntax for setting the start and end offsets. This lets developers adjust decoration spacing and create reveal effects with native text decorations instead of background gradients or additional elements. sampler: https://static.januschka.com/i-468928416/?asddsaasd MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/text-decoration-inset CL: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/chromium/src/+/7748204

Ecosystem Analysis: Part of CSS Text Decoration Module Level 4, text-decoration-inset introduces native inline offset controls for underlines, overlines, and strike-throughs. Cross-engine consensus is strong, with Firefox shipping the property first, followed by implementations across WebKit and Chromium. The feature resolves longstanding typographic fidelity limitations by eliminating the historical need for pseudo-element or background-gradient workarounds.

item.title: WebTransport receive stream — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport receive stream (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

Adds the standardized WebTransportReceiveStream interface, a ReadableStream subclass used for incoming unidirectional streams and the readable side of bidirectional streams. Its getStats() method returns per-stream byte counters: bytesReceived reports bytes received from the network, while bytesRead reports bytes delivered to the application.

Ecosystem Analysis: The WebTransport receive stream update standardizes the WebTransportReceiveStream interface across Chromium as a dedicated ReadableStream subclass, bringing Chromium into direct conformance with the W3C specification. By introducing the getStats() method, the API allows web applications to measure bytes received from the network against bytes consumed by JavaScript, dramatically simplifying backpressure diagnostics. Cross-engine consensus is strong, closing a long-standing platform discrepancy and harmonizing runtime types across modern browser implementations.

item.title: Long Animation Frames style and layout duration — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Long Animation Frames style and layout duration (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Add `styleDuration` and `forcedStyleDuration` information to the Long Animation Frame API, enabling developers to distinguish style and layout times.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Long Animation Frames API enhancement introduces discrete style and layout timings—such as `styleDuration` and `forcedStyleDuration`—enabling fine-grained diagnostics for CSS recalculations versus geometric layout thrashing. While Chromium and Microsoft Edge have spearheaded the capability toward general availability in Chrome 157 following origin trials, broader cross-engine support remains absent. Consequently, this serves as an advanced Chromium-centric telemetry enhancement rather than an interoperable baseline metric.

item.title: WebGPU: atomic-vec2u-min-max — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebGPU: atomic-vec2u-min-max (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Allows the use of 64-bit atomic minimum and maximum operations on `atomic<vec2u>` in WGSL. This provides WebGPU shader authors with a way to implement certain algorithms that use 64-bit atomics without requiring full support for 64-bit integers.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `atomic-vec2u-min-max` feature introduces 64-bit atomic minimum and maximum operations to WebGPU storage buffers using `atomic<vec2u>` as a composite surrogate type, sidestepping the current absence of native 64-bit integer arithmetic in WGSL. It specifically targets high-performance graphics techniques—such as Nanite-style compute rasterization and visibility buffers packing depth and material IDs—while maximizing cross-platform hardware reach across Metal, Vulkan, and Direct3D 12. The feature has established consensus within the W3C GPU for the Web Working Group and is shipping enabled by default in Chromium.

item.title: Web Bluetooth: Make BluetoothRemoteGATTServer an EventTarget — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Web Bluetooth: Make BluetoothRemoteGATTServer an EventTarget (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

BluetoothRemoteGATTServer inherits from EventTarget, exposing the standard addEventListener(), removeEventListener(), and dispatchEvent() methods. This enables connection-level events to be dispatched directly on the GATT server.

Ecosystem Analysis: Shipping enabled by default in Chrome 157, this change updates the BluetoothRemoteGATTServer interface to inherit directly from EventTarget, granting it standard addEventListener(), removeEventListener(), and dispatchEvent() capabilities. The change establishes the event plumbing necessary for connection-level notifications, most notably the separately proposed maxwritewithoutresponsesizechanged event for dynamic MTU handling. However, the feature exists entirely within Chromium's Web Bluetooth implementation, with no path toward broader web standardization.

item.title: Responsively-sized <iframe> — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Responsively-sized <iframe> (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Allow sites to opt into iframes having responsive sizing (sizing the <iframe> element in the parent document to the iframe document's layout overflow sizing, so that scrolling in the child document is avoided).

Ecosystem Analysis: Responsively-sized iframes, powered by the CSS frame-sizing property and a responsive-embedded-sizing meta tag, address the decades-old struggle of seamlessly sizing embedded documents without nested scrollbars or bespoke postMessage hacks. While Chromium has shipped the feature enabled by default in Chrome 154, the specification remains under active development in the W3C CSS Working Group. Cross-engine consensus is not yet reached, leaving the capability single-vendor for now.

item.title: Iterator Includes — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Iterator Includes (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

A TC39 proposal to allow the developer to ask whether an iterator yields a given value. Analogue to `Array.prototype.includes`.

Ecosystem Analysis: Iterator.prototype.includes bridges a long-standing ergonomics gap in JavaScript by allowing developers to lazily check whether an iterator yields a given value without converting it to an array. Championed through TC39 Stage 3, the feature has achieved unanimous engine consensus and shipped enabled by default in Chromium 154 and Firefox 154. With WebKit implementing support in Safari Technology Preview release notes, the API is rapidly approaching full cross-browser interoperability.

item.title: Local Network Access restrictions for Background Fetch — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Local Network Access restrictions for Background Fetch (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Background Fetch requests now require that the service worker's origin has the necessary Local Network Access (LNA) permission to send requests to local or loopback servers. This aligns Chromium's implementation with the intent of the Background Fetch spec, which states that such requests go through the Fetch spec and have the same security policies applied to them including, in this case, LNA checks. This prevents sites from bypassing LNA checks by using [Background Fetch spec](https://wicg.github.io/background-fetch/) instead of regular [Fetch](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/). For enterprises, you can use existing LNA enterprise policies in the same way you previously would have for regular Fetch API requests from service workers: - [LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut) - [LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls) - [LoopbackNetworkAllowedForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LoopbackNetworkAllowedForUrls) - [LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled) - [LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides)).

Ecosystem Analysis: Shipped in Chromium 154, this update closes a security bypass by subjecting Background Fetch requests initiated from service workers to the same Local Network Access (LNA) checks as standard fetch requests. While the Background Fetch API itself remains Chromium-only, closing this loophole harmonizes worker networking with the broader cross-engine drive to protect private and loopback networks from public origin abuse. Developer and security reception is generally supportive of the hardened attack surface, even though it adds architectural friction for legitimate intranet and companion daemon use cases.

item.title: Renewed HTML insertion&streaming methods — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Renewed HTML insertion&streaming methods (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Expose multiple HTML setting methods that provide a coherent story for dynamically inserting markup into an existing document. - Positional methods (before/after/append/prepend/replaceWith) that take HTML as argument, effectively replacing insertAdjacentHTML. - Streaming methods (stream{Append}HTML{Unsafe}) which return a WritableStream, receiving text as input and parsing HMHL. - Passing {runScripts} as part of SetHTMLUnsafeOptions, mimicking createContextualFragment behavior. - Supporting createParserOptions in trusted types, allowing trusted types to override scripting mode and sanitizer.

Ecosystem Analysis: The renewed HTML insertion and streaming methods modernize legacy DOM injection APIs by replacing disjointed primitives like insertAdjacentHTML with a symmetrical matrix of positional and streaming methods such as appendHTML and streamAppendHTML. Slated to ship enabled by default in Chrome 157 under the Declarative Partial Updates initiative, the suite standardizes built-in sanitization, explicit script execution via runScripts, and native WritableStream integration with Fetch streams. The broader web standards consensus is highly favorable, though cross-browser implementation timelines remain staggered.

item.title: Avoid caching module failures — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Avoid caching module failures (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

Currently web developers cannot retry failed module loads, as these failures are being cached (and retries just result in immediate failures). This change to the module loading behavior enables failed module loads to be manually retried (e.g. by calling `import()` again), solving real developer (and user) pain when it comes to using modules over unstable networks.

Ecosystem Analysis: The web platform has resolved a long-standing architectural pain point by removing transient network failures and HTTP errors from the browser's internal module map following WHATWG HTML PR #10327. Shipped by default in Chrome 156 with matching implementations landing across Firefox and WebKit (Safari Technology Preview), the feature transitions the platform from strict idempotency of failures to an availability-first model. This allows failed dynamic imports to be retried in-place without resorting to cache-busting URLs or disruptive full-page reloads.

item.title: Add options bag to WebSocket constructor — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Add options bag to WebSocket constructor (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Add support for passing an option bag (WebSocketInit dictionary) as the second argument to the WebSocket constructor. The option bag will initially support a "protocols" option, allowing developers to specify subprotocols (mirroring the existing protocols argument), and also serves as an extension point for future options. Before, this would be written `const socket = new WebSocket("wss://example.com:8080", "soap")`. After, this could also be written `const socket = new WebSocket("wss://example.com:8080", { protocols: "soap" })`. See https://github.com/whatwg/websockets/issues/42 and spec PR https://github.com/whatwg/websockets/pull/76 for this change.

Ecosystem Analysis: The addition of an options bag (WebSocketInit) to the WebSocket constructor modernizes the legacy API to mirror Fetch-like ergonomics and establishes an extensible foundation for modern networking features like Local Network Access (targetAddressSpace). Chromium has enabled the feature by default starting in Chrome 154, tracking WHATWG specification updates that maintain backwards compatibility with existing subprotocol strings. Cross-engine consensus is broadly favorable, with WebKit formally backing the specification change and Mozilla actively reviewing the proposal.

item.title: Window Shape API — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Window Shape API (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Window Shape API enables allowlisted [Isolated Web Apps](https://chromeos.dev/en/web/isolated-web-apps) on ChromeOS to have a customized window shape. By enabling non-rectangular and non-contiguous window layouts, developers can implement unique user experiences (such as widgets, floating panels, and overlays) that match the look-and-feel of native applications. The `window.setShape` API requires the window to be in _unframed_ display mode and requires the window-management permission to be granted. Administrators can manage this feature with existing policies for window management: - [DefaultWindowManagementSetting](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultWindowManagementSetting) configures the default state for the window management for all apps. The policies below can override this default. - [WindowManagementAllowedForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WindowManagementAllowedForUrls) allows IWAs with specified origins to enter unframed mode and set custom window shapes without any user interaction. - [WindowManagementBlockedForUrls](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WindowManagementBlockedForUrls) blocks the permission for specified origins, forcing Chrome to remove any custom window shapes and fallback to other available display modes.

Ecosystem Analysis: The Window Shape API (`window.setShape`) is a ChromeOS-specific capability designed strictly for allowlisted Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) operating in unframed display mode with window-management permissions. It enables developers to define non-rectangular and non-contiguous window boundaries using a series of bounding rectangles, unlocking desktop-native widgets, floating tools, and overlay interfaces. Because its explicit non-goals exclude standard web pages and other operating systems, it functions as an enterprise-managed platform extension rather than an open web standard.

item.title: Overscroll Areas — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Overscroll Areas (Chrome 157, Origin trial)

This feature adds a set of primitives to allow elements to anchor to overscroll areas of other elements. It further allows these elements to be revealed with swipe gestures, similar to scrollers.

Ecosystem Analysis: Overscroll Areas (incubating as Declarative Overscroll Actions in Open UI and advancing toward CSS Overscroll Behavior Module Level 2) introduces declarative primitives for gesture-driven UI patterns like drawer menus and bottom sheets. Currently advancing through Chromium prototyping and planned Origin Trials, the proposal seeks to offload swipe-to-reveal physics directly to compositor threads without complex JavaScript workarounds. However, formal cross-engine consensus remains at a very early stage, with neither Safari nor Firefox yet committing to an official stance.

item.title: Capability Elements Icon-only mode — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Capability Elements Icon-only mode (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Introduces a new attribute to render Capability Elements(<camera>, <microphone> and <geolocation>) as compact icon buttons without text using a `displaymode` attribute. This gives developers flexible UI density for spatial layouts such as map controls and video floating trays while preserving native security guarantees and full screen reader accessibility. This is an extension to the recently released Capability Elements https://chromestatus.com/feature/5153829504024576

Ecosystem Analysis: Shipping enabled by default in Chromium and Microsoft Edge 157, the icon-only mode adds a declarative `displaymode="icon-only"` attribute to Capability Elements such as `<camera>`, `<microphone>`, and `<geolocation>`. This iteration directly resolves longstanding layout friction where immutable localized text broke compact designs like map controls and video floating toolbars, while preserving browser-mediated clickjacking protections and screen-reader accessibility. However, because the capability elements model remains primarily a Chromium-driven effort, cross-engine interoperability is not yet established.

item.title: WebTransport reliability attributes — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport reliability attributes (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

Adds the WebTransport.reliability instance attribute and static WebTransport.supportsReliableOnly attribute. These APIs indicate whether the user agent supports WebTransport over exclusively reliable connections and whether an established session supports unreliable transport such as datagrams. In Chromium, reliability initially returns "pending" and changes to "supports-unreliable" after an HTTP/3 WebTransport connection is established.  Since Chromium does not currently support HTTP/2 fallback,  WebTransport.supportsReliableOnly returns false; any successfully established session uses HTTP/3 and supports unreliable datagrams.

Ecosystem Analysis: The `WebTransport.reliability` instance property and static `supportsReliableOnly` attribute provide runtime introspection to determine whether a browser or active connection supports unreliable datagrams over HTTP/3 versus strictly reliable fallback transports like HTTP/2. Standardized in the W3C WebTransport specification with cross-vendor participation, the API resolves to 'supports-unreliable' in Chromium where HTTP/3 is active and returns false for static reliable-only support. The feature provides a clean, forward-compatible contract for real-time web applications to adapt their transmission strategies.

item.title: object-fit and object-position apply to SVG documents in <object> and <embed> — Chrome 158 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
object-fit and object-position apply to SVG documents in <object> and <embed> (Chrome 158, Enabled by default)

SVG documents loaded through <object> or <embed> are sized and positioned inside the element's content box according to the CSS object-fit and object-position properties, the same way <img> content is. Previously Chrome ignored both properties for embedded SVG documents and always stretched the document viewport to the whole content box.

Ecosystem Analysis: By treating SVG documents embedded via <object> and <embed> elements as replaced elements, Chromium closes a longstanding specification gap in CSS Images and HTML rendering rules. This update brings Blink into direct parity with Gecko (Firefox), leaving WebKit (Safari) as the sole major rendering engine still stretching embedded SVGs regardless of CSS fit rules. Developers and standards contributors view the change as a major win for responsive vector graphics, eliminating awkward wrapper hacks previously needed for interactive SVG assets.

item.title: Remove FencedFrame element and window.fence APIs — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Remove FencedFrame element and window.fence APIs (Chrome 156, Deprecated)

Fenced frames are nested frames that embed content onto a page without the ability to share data between the fenced frame and its embedder. window.fence APIs include Fenced frames Ads reporting (FFAR) JS APIs that were created for privacy-safe ads reporting from FFs created using Protected Audience and SelectURL and getNestedConfigs() to support PA component ads. This intent is for removing both of these. Fenced frames element removal will be two step as detailed below. With the removal (or stub API replacement) of PA and selectURL, FFs can no longer be navigated and thus it is safe to remove them. Fenced frames are only able to be navigated using the urn:uuid in a FencedFrameConfig[1], which can only be created using the return values from runAdAuction and selectURL. These APIs are being deprecated and removed in M152 as per the following Intent threads: Protected Audience[2], Shared Storage[3]. Plan: Given that the fenced frames element can no longer be navigated, we propose removing the element from the code in the following phases: 1. M156: Keep the fenced frame element and its associated IDL dependencies as stubs. This is to ensure no JS call throws, e.g.calling fenced-frame-element.config.setSharedStorageContext(). 2. M156: In the same milestone we will also stub the window.fence APIs completely. Since there is no FF document navigation, these APIs cannot be invoked anymore, so it will be a no-op. 3. M157 Canary/Beta: Begin a controlled rollout of the stub FF HTML element removal via a field trial. Note that removing the element will resolve it to HTMLUnknownElement. At this point we are requesting approvals for all of the above steps. 4. M157 Stable: Assuming there are no regressions or breakage after reaching 1% stable, we will request additional approval for full removal of the FF element. [1]https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/fenced_frame/fenced_frame_config.idl [2]https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/k_nubsMb97g/m/awPD4IGLBAAJ [3]https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/uh5Ke6qyegc/m/WFTFnhyJBAAJ

Ecosystem Analysis: Chrome is deprecating and removing the `<fencedframe>` element and `window.fence` APIs across Chrome 156 and Chrome 157 following the sunset of prerequisite Privacy Sandbox auction APIs like Protected Audience and Shared Storage selectURL. Because fenced frames can no longer navigate without these upstream auction outputs, the container has become non-functional dead code within Blink. Since neither WebKit nor Gecko ever implemented the specification, removing it eliminates single-engine fragmentation with zero negative cross-browser compatibility risk.

item.title: Ask-before-HTTP warning on by default — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Ask-before-HTTP warning on by default (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

Chrome now prompts users by default when they access an insecure (HTTP) connection. IT admins can control this default behavior via [HttpsOnlyMode](https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode) policy.

Ecosystem Analysis: With Chrome 154 enabling the 'Ask-before-HTTP' interstitial by default on public hostnames, browsers are formally transitioning plain HTTP from a supported fallback to a deprecated security exception. The broader ecosystem strongly favors an encrypted-by-default web, building on years of passive warnings, automated HTTPS upgrades, and opt-in strict modes. Developer reception is largely supportive of eliminating unencrypted traffic, though friction has emerged around legacy infrastructure and intermediate URL forwarding.

item.title: Ship anchor-visible and anchor-valid, and deprecate the plural versions — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Ship anchor-visible and anchor-valid, and deprecate the plural versions (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

The CSSWG resolved to rename `anchors-valid` --> `anchor-valid` [1] and `anchors-visible` --> `anchor-visible` [2]. To accomplish this, we'll rename the properties to the singular variants, and add aliases from the plural versions to the singular versions. At a later date, we will remove the plural variants. This chromestatus is only about shipping the new versions, and deprecating the old ones (but not removing them). [1] https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/10201#issuecomment-4180411971 [2] https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/10201#issuecomment-4390233490

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS Working Group resolved to rename the position-visibility values from the plural anchors-visible and anchors-valid to the singular anchor-visible and anchor-valid to clarify that evaluations target a single default anchor. Chromium is shipping the singular keywords in Chrome 157 with backward-compatible aliases for the plural forms ahead of eventual deprecation. Major engine implementations are aligning around the singular syntax to achieve seamless cross-browser baseline interoperability for CSS Anchor Positioning.

item.title: Expose CSSStyleValue hierarchy to Worker contexts — Chrome 154 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
Expose CSSStyleValue hierarchy to Worker contexts (Chrome 154, Enabled by default)

The CSS Typed OM spec exposes the CSSStyleValue hierarchy to worker global scopes ([Exposed=(Window, Worker, PaintWorklet, LayoutWorklet)]), but Blink only exposed CSSStyleValue, CSSKeywordValue, CSSNumericValue, CSSUnitValue and CSSUnparsedValue to Window and the worklets. As a result these constructors were undefined in Workers, unlike in Firefox and Safari.

Ecosystem Analysis: Chrome 154 eliminates a longstanding interoperability gap by exposing the core CSS Typed OM hierarchy—including CSSStyleValue, CSSKeywordValue, CSSNumericValue, CSSUnitValue, and CSSUnparsedValue—to Worker global scopes. This change brings Chromium into full alignment with the CSS Typed OM Level 1 specification as well as Safari and Firefox, which already supported these interfaces off the main thread. With full multi-engine consensus achieved, developers can construct and calculate typed CSS primitives directly in web workers without cross-thread inconsistencies.

item.title: WebTransport Datagram writable streams and prioritization — Chrome 155 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
WebTransport Datagram writable streams and prioritization (Chrome 155, In developer trial (Behind a flag))

Adds the modern WebTransport Datagram sending API. WebTransportDatagramDuplexStream.createWritable() creates independent WebTransportDatagramsWritable streams. Each writable has mutable sendGroup and sendOrder attributes for expressing relative priority among queued WebTransport data in the same send group. Chromium currently applies this ordering among Datagram writables. The implementation also reports the negotiated maximum outgoing Datagram payload size and discards oversized writes as required by the WebTransport specification.

Ecosystem Analysis: WebTransport Datagram writable streams and prioritization modernize datagram egress by replacing the deprecated singleton writable stream with a factory method, `createWritable()`, returning independent `WebTransportDatagramsWritable` streams. This enables fine-grained scheduling via mutable `sendGroup` and `sendOrder` attributes and enforces payload limits by dropping oversized packets per the W3C WebTransport specification. Currently in developer trials behind flags in Chromium and targeted under Interop 2026, engine consensus is firmly aligned on standardizing this multi-stream prioritization model.

item.title: CORS enforcement for Background Fetch — Chrome 157 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CORS enforcement for Background Fetch (Chrome 157, Enabled by default)

Starting in Chrome 157, the Background Fetch API now enforces Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS). This update aligns Chromium's implementation with the intent of the [Background Fetch spec](https://wicg.github.io/background-fetch/). This ensures that Background Fetch requests are subject to the same security policies as regular Fetch requests, such as Local Network Access checks. This update prevents sites from bypassing CORS (and other security policy checks) by using Background Fetch instead of regular [Fetch](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/).

Ecosystem Analysis: Background Fetch remains a Chromium-only capability with limited web adoption, recently spared from deprecation after Chromium developers failed to reach consensus on removing it. Chromium is instead hardening the feature by migrating it from legacy download machinery into Blink's core fetch pipeline, strictly enforcing Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS), Local Network Access, and isolation policies by default in Chrome 157. Multi-engine consensus remains stalled, as neither WebKit nor Gecko plans to implement the underlying specification.

item.title: CSS random() function — Chrome 156 Ecosystem Update
item.description:
CSS random() function (Chrome 156, Enabled by default)

The random() function brings generative randomness to CSS, allowing web authors to generate a random numeric value within a specified range. For example, web authors can use random() to scatter elements randomly within their container: .dot { /* Position each dot randomly */ position: absolute; top: random(0%, 100%); left: random(0%, 100%); } This feature also includes caching controls. By default, each random() function resolves to a new, distinct value. Web authors can override this default by passing a <random-key> value as the function's first argument to control how random values are shared across properties and elements.

Ecosystem Analysis: The CSS random() function from the CSS Values and Units Module Level 5 is transitioning rapidly from an experimental capability into mainstream browser engines, shipping first in Safari and now landing by default in Chrome 156. Developers are enthusiastic about replacing brittle JavaScript math hacks and bloated Sass preprocessor loops with declarative, native generative randomness. Cross-engine consensus is strong, with Mozilla officially supportive of the CSS Working Group's standardized caching and scoping semantics while Gecko implementation is underway.
